assignments.title: 1.6 Critical Questions
assignments.html:
1.6 · Critical Questions
The Gothic Storm & Augustine, City of God
Tier 2/3 · short written responses · covers Lesson 1 + Primary Source 1
❓ QUESTIONS
1. Augustine says the barbarians' mercy toward those in churches should be “credited to the name of Christ.” What is he implying about the relationship between religious belief and the actual conduct of Alaric's army? Is this a claim about ideas causing behavior, material causes, or some combination? Explain, using this course's approach to historical causation.
2. Suppose Stilicho had not been executed in 408. Using what you know of his prior relationship with Alaric, argue for or against the claim that Rome would not have been sacked in 410. Defend your answer with reasoning, not just a guess.
3. Augustine wrote roughly a decade after the events he describes, for an audience that included both Christians and pagans. What does this tell you about how to read his account: is it a neutral record of what happened, or an argument built out of true facts? Does that make it less useful to a historian, or differently useful?
4. Identify one moment in this week's lesson where a different individual decision could plausibly have changed the outcome. Why does this course's approach to history ask you to notice moments like this, rather than treating Rome's fall as fated from the start?
📊 GRADING RUBRIC (25 pts)
Criteria Excellent (4) Proficient (3) Developing (2) Beginning (1)
Textual grounding
8 pts		 Cites specific language from Augustine and the lesson accurately. Uses the sources with minor imprecision. Vague or general reference to the sources. Little or no use of the sources.
Quality of reasoning
10 pts		 Builds a clear, well-supported argument; counterfactual reasoning is specific and historically grounded. Argument is reasonable but underdeveloped in places. Argument is asserted rather than reasoned. No real argument is offered.
Historical understanding
7 pts		 Demonstrates command of causation, contingency, and the difference between ideas and material causes. Shows solid understanding with a gap or two. Shows partial understanding. Shows little understanding of the concepts.
Total:
25 pts total

assignments.title: 1.9 Primary Source Exercise
assignments.html:
1.9 · Primary Source Exercise
Vandals, Attila, and Jordanes' Getica
Tier 3 · open-ended written exercise · covers Lesson 2 + Primary Source 2 · this week's signature assessment
❓ QUESTIONS
1. Jordanes says Attila's nation was “won by him alone” through a mix of “craft and simplicity.” Compare this personal, one-man model of political power to the institutional model of the Roman state described in this week's lessons. Which model can better survive the ruler's death, and why?
2. Suppose Aetius had lost, rather than won, at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains in 451, and Attila had gone on to conquer much of Gaul. Would the collapse of Western Rome likely have happened faster, slower, or in roughly the same way it actually did? Defend your answer with specific reasoning about what Attila's empire was and was not capable of sustaining.
3. What is the significance of Odoacer sending the imperial regalia to Constantinople rather than simply keeping it or destroying it? What does this act suggest about how contemporaries understood the relationship between the Western and Eastern halves of the empire in 476?
4. This lesson argues that the fall of the West was “a whimper, not a bang.” Using evidence from both this week's lessons, explain what continued (institutions, culture, local government) and what changed after 476. Is “fall” the right word for what happened, or would you choose a different one? Defend your choice.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC (25 pts)
Criteria Excellent (4) Proficient (3) Developing (2) Beginning (1)
Use of sources
8 pts		 Draws precisely on Jordanes and the lesson; distinguishes legend from likely fact. Uses sources accurately with minor gaps. General or imprecise use of sources. Minimal use of sources.
Alternative-path reasoning
10 pts		 Constructs a specific, historically grounded alternative and defends it against objections. Offers a reasonable counterfactual with some development. Counterfactual is asserted without real support. No genuine counterfactual reasoning attempted.
Historical judgment
7 pts		 Shows sophisticated understanding of continuity, change, and contingency; avoids treating the fall as either inevitable or a single event. Shows solid understanding with a minor lapse. Shows partial understanding. Shows little understanding.
Total:
25 pts total

assignments.title: 1.10 VR Activity: Exhibit One: Rome Besieged
assignments.html:
VR Activity
Exhibit One: Rome Besieged
Solo · one in-headset session
🎯 WHAT YOU'RE DOING

You will visit a reconstruction of Rome's Aurelian Walls and the Forum to see the scale of what Alaric's army confronted, then arrange evidence into your first Frontier Atlas exhibit panel: a case for what actually caused the sack of 410.

💻 WHAT YOU'LL NEED
▶
A VR headset (or desktop/mobile VR client)
▶
Completion of Lesson 1 and Lesson 2 before starting
▶
About 25 minutes
🔒 HOW TO JOIN
Device: VR headset preferred; desktop/mobile supported.
Session type: Temporary Session (solo).
Session ID: WH9-Q1-W01-VR (posted in Canvas).
Location: Roman Forum & Aurelian Walls, Late Antiquity.
Spawn point: You will arrive at the Portal Spawn Point just outside the Walls; a Sticky Note there gives your first instruction.
📝 WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
1
Walk the Aurelian Walls and note their scale using the placed image comparing the walls to a modern building.
2
Open the pre-placed interactive whiteboard titled “Three Causes,” and use the 3D pen or the Drawpad to write the three causes from this week's lessons (Adrianople, decades of failed accommodation, Stilicho's execution) in the order you judge most decisive to least.
3
Place a Sticky Note on the Whiteboard defending your ranking in two or three sentences.
4
Record a 60–90 second spatial recording standing at the Walls, explaining your ranking aloud: this becomes Exhibit 1 of your Frontier Atlas.
📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT

Submit the spatial recording link (or a screen recording of it) to the Week 1 VR Activity assignment in Canvas, along with a one-sentence caption for your exhibit panel.

Estimated time: About 25 minutes

✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
Walked the Location and used the placed display
☐
Wrote and ranked all three causes on the Whiteboard
☐
Recorded and submitted the spatial recording with a caption
👨‍🏫 FACILITATOR NOTE

Students commonly want to rank causes by which felt most dramatic (the sack itself) rather than most decisive (Stilicho's execution). Encourage them to defend their ranking rather than simply restating the lesson; there is no single correct order, but the reasoning should show real engagement with contingency.

assignments.title: 1.14 Critical Questions
assignments.html:
1.14 · Critical Questions
New Rome in the East & Procopius, History of the Wars
Tier 2/3 · short written responses · covers Lesson 1 + Primary Source 1
❓ QUESTIONS
1. Theodora tells Justinian that “royalty is a good burial-shroud” rather than fleeing the Nika riots. Using the Classical Republican standard of judgment from the world history skill (can a regime maintain internal order and command loyalty under threat?), evaluate Justinian's regime based on this episode. Did it pass or fail this test, and on what evidence?
2. Suppose Justinian and Theodora had fled Constantinople by boat, as the emperor's advisors initially urged. How might Byzantine history (and the later reconquests and legal reforms you will read about tomorrow) have unfolded differently? Defend your answer using details from both this source and Lesson 1.
3. Is Theodora's role in this episode more consistent with a Great-Man (or Great-Woman) view of history, or a structural/institutional view? Explain your reasoning, citing specific details from Procopius's account.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC (25 pts)
Criteria Excellent (4) Proficient (3) Developing (2) Beginning (1)
Textual grounding
8 pts		 Cites Procopius and the lesson precisely. Uses sources accurately with minor gaps. General reference only. Minimal use of sources.
Quality of reasoning
9 pts		 Argument is specific, well-supported, and engages counter-considerations. Reasonable argument, some development. Argument asserted, not reasoned. No real argument.
Historical judgment
8 pts		 Applies the Classical Republican standard and the Great-Man framework accurately and critically. Applies frameworks with minor confusion. Partial application. Frameworks not meaningfully applied.

25 pts total

assignments.title: 1.17 VR Activity: Exhibit Two: Justinian's Constantinople

VR Activity
Exhibit Two: Justinian's Constantinople
Solo · one in-headset session
🎯 WHAT YOU'RE DOING

You will visit a reconstruction of the Hagia Sophia and Constantinople's walls, place evidence from this week's readings, and argue the week's central question directly: was Byzantium a true continuation of Rome, or something new? This is this week's signature assessment.

💻 WHAT YOU'LL NEED
▶
A VR headset (or desktop/mobile VR client)
▶
Completion of both lessons and both primary sources before starting
▶
About 30 minutes
🔒 HOW TO JOIN
Device: VR headset preferred; desktop/mobile supported.
Session type: Temporary Session (solo).
Session ID: WH9-Q1-W02-VR (posted in Canvas).
Location: Hagia Sophia & Theodosian Walls, Constantinople, 6th century.
Spawn point: You arrive inside the Hagia Sophia beneath the great dome; a Sticky Note gives your first instruction.
📝 WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
1
Look up at the dome and use the placed image to compare its scale to other ancient buildings you have studied.
2
Walk to the Theodosian Walls exhibit area and examine the interactive map showing Belisarius's reconquest of North Africa and Italy.
3
Open the interactive whiteboard titled “Continuation or Departure?” and place two columns of sticky notes: evidence Byzantium continued Rome (law, titles, reconquest) and evidence it became something new (language, religion-and-throne fused together, geography).
4
Add the line from Justinian's Institutes you read today (“to live honestly, to hurt no one, to give everyone his due”) to whichever column you judge it belongs, and justify the placement with a second sticky note.
5
Record a 90-second to 2-minute spatial recording at the Whiteboard arguing your final verdict: continuation, departure, or a genuine mixture, and why. This is Exhibit 2 of your Frontier Atlas.
📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT

Submit your spatial recording link (or a screen recording) and a one-sentence exhibit caption to the Week 2 VR Activity assignment in Canvas.

Estimated time: About 30 minutes

✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
Examined both the dome and the reconquest interactive map
☐
Populated both columns of the Whiteboard with specific evidence
☐
Placed and justified the Institutes quotation
☐
Recorded and submitted a clear final verdict with reasoning
👨‍🏫 FACILITATOR NOTE

This is the week's substantive, teacher-graded assessment (Tier 3), so give students real time to work through the Whiteboard before recording. There is no single correct verdict; look for students engaging both columns of evidence rather than picking a side reflexively. Be ready to demonstrate placing a Sticky Note if a student is stuck on the mechanics.

assignments.title: 2.6 Critical Questions
assignments.html:
2.6 · Critical Questions
Roots of England & Gregory of Tours
Tier 2/3 · short written responses · covers Lesson 1 + Primary Source 1
❓ QUESTIONS
1. Gregory of Tours reports that Clovis converted after praying for victory in battle, and that his army converted with him. What does this suggest about the relationship between religious conviction and political/military calculation in early medieval conversion stories? Is it possible (and historically responsible) to hold that both genuine belief and practical advantage were operating together in Clovis's decision?
2. Suppose Clovis had converted to Arian Christianity (like many other Germanic kings of his time) rather than Catholic Christianity. How might this have changed his relationship with the Gallo-Roman population he ruled, who were themselves Catholic? Use specific reasoning about religious alignment and political legitimacy.
3. Using Bede's term “the English people” and the Heptarchy's continued political division, explain the difference between a cultural/religious nation and a political state. Can you think of a modern example where these two things are similarly out of step with each other?
📊 GRADING RUBRIC (25 pts)
Criteria Excellent (4) Proficient (3) Developing (2) Beginning (1)
Textual grounding
8 pts		 Cites Gregory of Tours and the lesson precisely. Minor imprecision. General reference only. Minimal use.
Quality of reasoning
9 pts		 Specific, well-supported argument engaging complexity. Reasonable, some development. Asserted, not reasoned. No real argument.
Historical judgment

assignments.title: 2.9 Primary Source Exercise
assignments.html:
2.9 · Primary Source Exercise
Roots of France & Bede's Ecclesiastical History
Tier 3 · open-ended written exercise · covers Lesson 2 + Primary Source 2
❓ QUESTIONS
1. Bede notes that King Aethelberht took precautions against “magical arts” before meeting Augustine's mission. What does this detail suggest about how a pagan Anglo-Saxon king likely understood the arrival of a new religion, and how does it complicate any simple story of conversion as either purely spiritual awakening or purely political calculation?
2. Suppose Clovis had converted to Arianism rather than Catholicism in 496. Using the reasoning from this week's Lesson 2, argue whether the Frankish kingdom would likely have expanded as successfully across Gaul, or whether it might have shared the fate of the Visigothic or Vandal kingdoms. Defend your answer.
3. Compare the conversion of Kent (Bede) and the conversion of the Franks (Gregory of Tours, earlier this week). What common pattern do you see in how early medieval kings and their peoples adopted Christianity? What does this pattern suggest about the relationship between political authority and religious change in this period?
4. This module's standards ask you to trace the beginnings of English and French national identity. Based on both lessons this week, would you say a Frank in 550 or an Anglo-Saxon in 650 thought of themselves primarily as members of a nation, a kingdom, a religious community, or a kin group? Defend your answer with evidence.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC (25 pts)
Criteria Excellent (4) Proficient (3) Developing (2) Beginning (1)
Use of sources
8 pts		 Precise, comparative use of both primary sources. Accurate with minor gaps. General use. Minimal use.
Alternative-path reasoning

Quarter 1 Capstone Project
The Frontier Atlas of Christendom, c. 1100–1204
Tier 3 · VR component + written component · due at the end of Quarter 1
🎯 PROJECT OVERVIEW

Across Quarter 1 you built nine VR exhibits, one nearly every week, documenting a people, ruler, or institution on the frontiers of Rome's heirs: the Western Empire's fall, Byzantium's survival, the Anglo-Saxon and Frankish kingdoms, the rise of Islam, the Carolingian world, feudalism and monasticism, England's conquest, the Investiture Controversy, and the Crusades. This capstone asks you to bring all nine together into a single gallery walk and to argue, using the whole quarter's evidence, what actually held medieval Christendom's frontiers together: and what put them most at risk.

🎯 ESSENTIAL QUESTION
Across three centuries of collapse, conquest, and contact, what made a medieval frontier hold, and what made it break?

assignments.html:
9.17 · Capstone Project
Turning Points: A World Remade, 1206–1648
Tier 3 · VR component + written component · due at the end of Quarter 2
🎯 PROJECT OVERVIEW

Across Quarter 2 you built six Turning Points exhibits: the Mongol Storm, the Black Death, Constantinople Encircled, Florence, Wittenberg, and the Two Thomases. This week's lessons add a seventh, unbuilt turning point (the Thirty Years War and the Peace of Westphalia) for you to add yourself. This final capstone asks you to assemble all seven into one gallery and to answer, using the whole semester's evidence from Week 1 to Week 18, this course's central historiographical question.

🎯 ESSENTIAL QUESTION
Across nearly twelve centuries, from the fall of Rome to the Peace of Westphalia, what actually drives historical change: the deliberate designs of great figures, the slow pressure of ideas and material conditions, or contingency: particular people making particular choices that could easily have gone otherwise?
💻 VR COMPONENT: GALLERY ASSEMBLY
1
Join the persistent Gallery Session at Session ID WH9-Q2-CAPSTONE-VR (posted in Canvas).
2
Build the seventh alcove: The Thirty Years War using this week's lessons and the Treaty of Westphalia excerpt: place an image or diagram and a Sticky Note or brief recording summarizing the war's causes and Westphalia's significance.
3
Arrange all seven Turning Points alcoves in chronological order in the Gallery Location's numbered spaces, each displaying its title, an image or diagram, and your reflection.
4
Add a final, eighth alcove: “Verdict.” Using an interactive whiteboard, write your answer to the essential question above, citing evidence from at least five different Turning Points, and at least one example from Quarter 1's Frontier Atlas.
5
Record a 4–5 minute spatial recording walking the full gallery in chronological order, narrating your argument, and arriving at your final verdict.
📝 WRITTEN COMPONENT (M365 Word Document)

Write a 700–900 word essay answering the essential question directly, citing specific evidence from at least five Turning Points and at least one example from Quarter 1. Your essay should explicitly weigh the three historiographical frameworks this course has used all semester (Great Men and Great Events, the history of ideas and material conditions, and contingency) and should reach a defended conclusion about which explains the semester's history best, or how they work together.

questions.text: What event most directly triggered the crisis that led to the Battle of Adrianople (378)?

answers.text: A planned Gothic invasion of the Balkans
Roman mismanagement of Gothic refugees fleeing the Huns
A succession dispute in the Roman court
An Arian-Catholic theological dispute

questions.text: Which of the following best explains why Stilicho's execution in 408 mattered?

It converted Alaric to Catholic Christianity
It had no significant effect

The Senate house
Christian churches
Grain warehouses

Pure bad luck with no political dimension
A single inevitable law of imperial decline operating for centuries
The empire's abandonment of the old Roman gods a generation earlier

About 30 years
About 800 years

It was closer to Rome than any other city
It had no prior history or population

questions.text: What happened to the Roman Empire's administrative structure in 395?

answers.text: It was permanently and formally abolished
It moved entirely to Constantinople
It was divided between two sons of Theodosius as an administrative arrangement, not intended as a permanent split
It was restored to a single Republic

questions.text: What did the Byzantines call themselves, and what does this suggest about how they understood their own state?

Constantinopolitans; their identity was purely local to the city

The existence of an emperor

discussions.html:
This module's lessons argued that Rome's sack in 410 was not the inevitable collapse of an ancient empire. Charlemagne could barely write his own name, yet he sponsored a deliberate revival of Latin learning, script, and church reform that historians now call the Carolingian Renaissance. discussions.html:

discussions.title: 6.17 Discussion: The Yuan Dynasty of China
discussions.html:
Kublai Khan governed China less like a raiding steppe warlord and more like a settled emperor: he founded the Yuan Dynasty and adopted Chinese court forms, while keeping the Mongol elite at the top of a new social order. His two invasions of Japan, however, both failed completely, and he never attempted a third.

discussions.title: 7.24 Discussion: The Council of Florence
discussions.html:
The 1439 Council of Florence tried to reunite the Eastern and Western churches after centuries of division, largely so a desperate Byzantine emperor could win Western military help against the advancing Ottomans. discussions.title: 9.20 Discussion: Galileo and the New Physics
discussions.html:
Galileo Galilei was, for years, on friendly terms with Pope Urban VIII, an admirer of his work. Their relationship broke down after Galileo's 1632 Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems, whose defender of the traditional geocentric view was widely read at the papal court as a mocking caricature of the Pope's own arguments. The Roman Inquisition tried Galileo the following year and forced him to recant.
